title: Interactive scheduler tuning playbook
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a practical, human-in-the-loop playbook for tuning the continuous batching scheduler. Goal: give an engineer a short checklist and interactive workflow to iterate on batch_size/timeout/fairness knobs while understanding tail behavior and throughput tradeoffs. This is explicitly not a final experimental report — it should live alongside quick runs, profiling snippets, and decisions made during paired-debugging sessions.

When to use this playbook:
- New workload pattern appears in production (e.g., sudden increase in small requests).
- Tail latency SLO (p95/p99) regressing after a model rollout or infra change.
- Need a quick rollback path while further experiments run.

Assumptions and instrumentation required:
- Scheduler exposes: max_batch_size, target_latency_ms (soft timeout), fairness_mode (age-based | size-priority | hybrid), preemption_enabled (bool), max_batch_wait_ms (hard cap).
- Runtime metrics available per model-route: batch_formed_size_histogram, batch_wait_time_histogram, tokens_per_batch, latency_per_request (queue+inference), cpu/gpu_util_pct, kv_cache_hit_rate, evict_count.
- Tracing hooks: request_id -> batch_id mapping, start/queue/infer/end timestamps.
- Profiling tools: per-step flame (py-spy or perf), GPU kernel timeline from nvprof/nsight, scheduler debug logs (batch opened/closed events).

Quick interactive workflow (30-90m loop):
1) Baseline capture (10-20m)
   - Switch canary traffic to run under an isolated config.
   - Capture 10-20 minutes of steady traffic or synthetic replay matching current QPS pattern.
   - Capture: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency, batch size distribution, batch wait distribution, throughput (reqs/s), gpu_util.
   - Save snapshot with timestamped name e.g., "snap-20250203-canary-10m".

2) Short hypotheses (5-10m)
   - Read metrics and ask: are there many tiny batches (median batch size < 30% of max)? If yes, suspect timeout too low or batching window starved.
   - Is p99 dominated by queue waiting or inference? Compare queue_time vs infer_time. If queue_time >> infer_time, scheduling is culprit.

3) Fast experiment set A: timeout sweep (20-40m)
   - Run 3 short runs (5–10m each) varying target_latency_ms: current, +2x, -50%. Keep max_batch_size fixed.
   - Collect batch_wait_histograms and tail latencies.
   - Expected observations: increasing timeout increases batch sizes and throughput, but p50 may increase; decreasing timeout reduces p50 but may increase small-batch overhead and p99.
   - Decision rule: if p99 is queue-dominated and increasing timeout reduces p99 without blowing up p50 beyond SLO, adopt larger timeout and mark for longer run.

4) Fast experiment set B: max_batch_size sweep (20-40m)
   - Try current, +25%, +100% max_batch_size. Timeout unchanged.
   - Watch for diminishing returns: if tokens_per_batch plateaus or gpu_util saturates and latency worsens, larger batches are harmful.

5) Fairness probe (15-30m)
   - Toggle fairness_mode: age-based vs size-priority vs hybrid. Run short (10m) replay with mixed request sizes (short/long).
   - Inspect per-class tail latencies: small requests often suffer under pure size-priority. Age-based protects small requests but can reduce aggregate throughput.
   - Instrumentation: compute fairness metric = p99_small / p99_large. Aim for fairness metric <= 2 unless product requires stricter isolation.

6) Microburst and preemption checks (ongoing)
   - Enable preemption_enabled if supported. Run a synthetic microburst (spike 5x for 30s) to validate preemption reduces tail. Capture flakiness.

7) Deep dive profiling (as-needed)
   - If queue waiting still explains tails: enable trace sampling (1% of requests) with request->batch timeline. Look for pathological interleaving or lock contention in scheduler.
   - If inference time has long tails: collect GPU kernel timelines and check for kernel fallback, memory thrashing, or copy stalls.

Result recording and rollback plan:
- After each short run store a 1-line result: config, snapshot id, p50/p95/p99, median batch_size, notes. Keep entries short and tabular (CSV pasted into Drive).
- If a change improves p99 by >= 10% and doesn't increase p50 beyond SLO, promote to "staged" and run a 4h stability window.
- If a change regresses any monitored SLO by >10%, immediately revert to last-known-good and attach failure snapshot.

Common patterns and suggested knobs (opinionated):
- Sparse small requests (<10 tokens) dominated workloads: favor lower timeout + age-based fairness to protect small requests, or enable tiny-batch cache.
- Dense long-token workloads: increase max_batch_size aggressively; raise timeout to let batches fill. Watch GPU memory and per-batch token count.
- Mixed workloads: hybrid fairness + moderate timeout (1.5x baseline) often balances fairness and unit cost.

Example quick log entry format (copy/paste into Drive):
2025-02-03T14:22Z, snap-20250203-canary-10m, config: timeout=12ms,max_bs=128,fair=hybrid, p50=18ms,p95=56ms,p99=148ms, med_batch=40,notes=timeout up -> p99 down 18%

Troubleshooting checklist (if experiments not resolving tails):
- Are traces showing many aborted batches (open->evict)? If yes, investigate eviction heuristics and memory pressure.
- Is KV cache hit rate low causing repeated compute? Consider cache warming or route pinning.
- Are there long GC pauses or Python GIL stalls visible in flame graphs? Try moving scheduler off Python thread or increase host CPU.
- GPU-related: kernel fallback, mixed-precision instability, or contiguous memory fragmentation. Collect nsight timelines.

Notes on reproducibility and safety:
- Avoid running experiments across operator changes (e.g., scheduler binary update) unless one is explicitly testing that change. Keep config-only changes separated.
- Always attach a revertable config and a health-check runbook for on-call.

Open questions / next steps (up for discussion):
- Can we expose a "synthetic interleaving mode" in the scheduler that forces pathological interleavings to test fairness across many seeds?
- Should we add a per-route suggested default profile derived from traffic clustering (burstiness index)?
- Automate the short-run decision rules: could a small controller recommend next knob sweep automatically? Feels like a low-effort win.

Appendix: handy commands and locations
- Collect metrics snapshot: ./tools/collect_metrics --route <route> --duration 10m --out snap-<ts>.tar
- Run microburst harness: ./tools/microburst --qps <x> --duration 30s --payload-mix small:70,large:30
- Quick trace sample: ./tools/trace_sample --rate 1% --out trace-<ts>.json
- Relevant git/GH: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/tree/main/scheduler
- Related ticket: JIRA:INFR-1294 (scheduler fairness investigation)

Author notes: this playbook grew out of paired-debug sessions during the December 2024 incident where a model rollout caused p99 regressions for low-latency routes. Keep concise logs; the value is in quick iteration and readable snapshots.

End of playbook.
